column1: Six development-team scenarios. Decide what collaboration actually calls for, not what sounds polite.
Back to the Topic 1.1 lessonAll Big Idea 1 topics
The lesson quiz asks what pair programming is. These ask you to sit inside a team that is going wrong and pick the move that fixes it.

column1: Two students build a fitness app. One writes every line while the other watches, and they never swap.
They call this pair programming. What is the strongest reason it is not?
Correct. Pair programming is a driver who types and a navigator who reviews, questions, and catches errors, with the roles rotating. Watching passively is neither role.
Incorrect. Two people on one machine is the normal form of pair programming, not a violation of it.
Incorrect. Pair programming works in person or online. The medium is not what makes it collaboration.
Incorrect. Pair programming is specifically two people. Team size is not the defect here.
A team of four ships a campus map app. Every tester was a member of the team.
Which consequence is the most likely and the most specific to that testing choice?
Incorrect. Testing practices and copyright are unrelated concerns.
Incorrect. Who tests a program has no bearing on its running speed.
Incorrect. Syntax errors are caught by the language, not by the diversity of the test group.
Correct. This is the core argument for collaboration in CSP. A group that shares a perspective shares its blind spots, so unmet needs and untested situations survive testing.
Two teammates disagree about whether the app should open on a map or on a search box.
Which response best demonstrates consensus building rather than simply winning?
Incorrect. Deferring to seniority ends the disagreement without ever examining the reasons, which is not consensus.
Incorrect. A coin flip discards both arguments. It is fast, not collaborative.
Correct. Consensus building means surfacing the reasons, finding shared criteria, and deciding against those criteria. The user need is the shared criterion here.
Incorrect. Carrying both designs defers the decision and doubles the maintenance rather than resolving anything.
A student says a wooden chair with a QR code sticker is a computing innovation.
What is the correct classification, and why?
Incorrect. Something being scannable by a computer does not make a program integral to the object. The chair is a chair with or without the sticker.
Correct. A computing innovation requires a program as an integral part of its function. Remove the code from the chair and it still works exactly as a chair.
Incorrect. Nonphysical computing innovations are things like e-commerce or social media. A sticker on furniture is neither.
Incorrect. Being designed with computer assistance does not make the product itself a computing innovation.
A team keeps their program notes, decisions, and open questions in a shared online document.
Which benefit of that practice is the one AP CSP specifically credits?
Correct. Collaboration tools carry the reasoning, not just the result, which is what lets a teammate or a later developer pick the work up without redoing the thinking.
Incorrect. Program documentation and in-code comments serve overlapping but different purposes, and neither removes the need for the other.
Incorrect. Documentation is written for people. It does not change what the machine does at runtime.
Incorrect. Accessibility comes from deliberate design choices in the program, not from keeping notes.
During a conflict, one teammate goes quiet and stops contributing for two work sessions.
Which action best applies the interpersonal skills the CED names for collaboration?
Incorrect. Waiting is not conflict resolution. The behavior is already the signal that something needs a conversation.
Incorrect. Escalating to a grade is neither communication nor negotiation, and it does not restore the collaboration.
Incorrect. Routing around a person keeps the project moving and leaves the conflict entirely unaddressed.
Correct. Communication, conflict resolution, and negotiation are the named skills. Asking, listening, then renegotiating uses all three.

ap-csp-course-bi1-program-function-purpose-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 1.2 Exercise 2: Program Function and Purpose Applied Challenge","<style>
Six scenarios that separate what a program is FOR from what it DOES, which is where most exam points are lost.
Back to the Topic 1.2 lessonAll Big Idea 1 topics
Purpose, function, input, output, and behavior get used loosely in conversation and precisely on the exam. These force the precise reading.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: An app takes a photo of a plant and names the species.
Which statement describes the program's PURPOSE rather than its function?
Incorrect. That is the function: the how. Purpose is the why.
Correct. Purpose answers why the program exists and what problem it solves for a person. The mechanism is not mentioned.
Incorrect. An input is a component of the function, not the purpose.
Incorrect. An output is a component of the function, not the purpose.
A program asks for a temperature in Celsius and displays it in Fahrenheit. Which pair correctly identifies its input and output?
Correct. Input is data the program receives, output is data it produces. The user supplies Celsius, the program produces Fahrenheit.
Incorrect. This reverses the flow described in the prompt.
Incorrect. Keyboard and screen are devices. Input and output name the DATA, not the hardware carrying it.
Incorrect. The formula is part of how the program works, not data supplied to it.
Two students describe the same quiz program.
Student 1 says it teaches vocabulary. Student 2 says it displays a word, reads a typed answer, and keeps a running score. What is the correct characterization?
Incorrect. Only one of the two describes purpose. The other is a step by step account of behavior.
Incorrect. Describing the same program does not make both descriptions the same kind of description.
Incorrect. This reverses the two. Teaching vocabulary is the goal, not the mechanism.
Correct. Purpose is the problem being solved for the user. Function is the input, process, and output that solve it.
A weather app shows a different home screen in the morning than in the evening.
Which term best describes that difference?
Incorrect. It produces output at both times. The output is simply different.
Incorrect. The purpose, helping a user plan around weather, is unchanged. Only what it shows changes.
Correct. Behavior is what the program does for a given input. Time of day is an input, so different input yields different behavior.
Incorrect. One program responding differently to different input is not two functions.
A tip calculator returns 0 whenever the bill total is left blank.
Which description of the situation is most accurate?
Incorrect. Purpose is a property of the program, not of one input. It does not disappear on an empty field.
Correct. The program does something specific and predictable for blank input. That is defined behavior, and the fix is to handle the input rather than to call it a crash.
Incorrect. A syntax error prevents the program from running at all, not just for one input.
Incorrect. It produces output. The output is 0, which is exactly the problem.
Which of these is the clearest statement of a program's purpose for the Create Task written response?
Correct. A purpose statement names the user and the problem solved, in terms someone outside the class could follow.
Incorrect. The language and timeline describe the development process, not the purpose.
Incorrect. A procedure signature is an implementation detail.
Incorrect. These are language features, which belong in a different part of the response.

Six scenarios inside an iterative development cycle. Pick the next move, not the ideal one in hindsight.
Back to the Topic 1.3 lessonAll Big Idea 1 topics
Development is investigate, design, prototype, test, and repeat. These questions drop you at a specific point in that cycle and ask what comes next.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A team has an idea for a study timer and starts by writing the full final version.
Which criticism of that approach is the one the development process in CSP is built to prevent?
Incorrect. Language features are available at every stage of development.
Incorrect. Line count is not the concern. Discovering a design mistake late is.
Correct. Iterative development exists so that a wrong assumption surfaces after a small investment rather than a large one.
Incorrect. Prototypes are not faster at runtime than finished programs.
Testing reveals users want a pause button nobody planned for.
Where does that discovery belong in the development process?
Incorrect. A bug is a program not doing what it was designed to do. This is the design itself being incomplete.
Correct. Iteration means testing feeds back into design. An unmet user need discovered in testing is exactly what that feedback loop is for.
Incorrect. Deferring every unplanned need until the end defeats the purpose of iterating.
Incorrect. The purpose, helping users manage study time, still holds. Only the requirements grew.
Which pair of program requirements is stated most usefully for development?
Correct. Each clause names an observable behavior, so a tester can determine whether it happens.
Incorrect. Better is a comparison with no criterion attached.
Incorrect. These are code quality practices, not requirements about what the program does.
Incorrect. Fast and easy are goals without a test. Nothing here says when they are met.
A developer keeps a development log noting what was tried, what failed, and why.
Which is the strongest argument for that log in a collaborative project?
Incorrect. Documentation is written alongside the program and does not change its length.
Incorrect. Testing has no such prerequisite.
Incorrect. Attribution is a real use of a log, but it is not what makes it valuable to development.
Correct. A record of dead ends is the part of the reasoning that is otherwise lost, and it is exactly what a collaborator needs to avoid repeating the work.
A team is deciding what to build first for a school event app.
Which approach best matches the design phase as CSP describes it?
Incorrect. Building everything badly first spreads effort thin and delays discovering which features matter.
Incorrect. Ease of implementation is a real consideration, but it does not tell you whether anyone needs the feature.
Correct. Investigating user needs before designing is the step that keeps development anchored to a purpose.
Incorrect. Another app was designed for another set of users, whose needs may not match.
Two teammates each wrote a version of the same procedure without knowing the other had.
Which practice would most directly have prevented this?
Incorrect. Testing finds defects in code that exists. It does not prevent duplicate work.
Correct. Duplicated effort is a collaboration failure, and an agreed division of responsibility recorded up front is the specific practice that prevents it.
Incorrect. Comments explain code after it is written, which is too late here.
Incorrect. Algorithm choice has nothing to do with two people writing the same thing.

ap-csp-course-bi1-identifying-correcting-errors-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 1.4 Exercise 2: Identifying and Correcting Errors Applied Challenge","<style>
Six broken programs. Name the error type, then pick the fix that actually addresses it.
Back to the Topic 1.4 lessonAll Big Idea 1 topics
Naming an error is half the skill. These pair each error with candidate fixes, most of which change something real and still leave the bug in place.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A program is meant to display the average of three numbers but always displays a value near the first number. Which error type is this?
Incorrect. Overflow is about values exceeding what can be stored, which is not happening here.
Incorrect. The expression is valid. Nothing prevents it from being parsed or run.
Correct. The program runs to completion and produces a wrong answer, which is the definition of a logic error. Only c is divided by 3.
Incorrect. Runtime errors stop execution. This finishes and prints something.
A program crashes with a message about an invalid index whenever the list is empty.
Which classification and fix pair is correct?
Incorrect. A logic error produces a wrong result without stopping. This stops.
Correct. The program halts during execution on certain input, which is a runtime error, and guarding the access before it happens is the direct fix.
Incorrect. A syntax error would prevent the program from running at all, including on non empty lists.
Incorrect. Overflow concerns value size, not an access past the end of a list.
A student adds a DISPLAY statement inside a loop to see what a variable holds on each pass.
Which best describes what that technique accomplishes?
Correct. Debugging by inspecting intermediate values narrows a wrong final answer down to the specific step where it first diverged.
Incorrect. Adding output does not change what kind of error is present.
Incorrect. A program with a syntax error would not have run far enough to print anything, but printing is not how you check for one.
Incorrect. Displaying a value never changes it. The bug is untouched.
A team fixes a bug by adding a special case that returns the right answer for the one input they tested.
Incorrect. Conditionals for special cases are perfectly valid. The problem is what this one hides.
Incorrect. Nothing in the described fix creates a syntax error.
Incorrect. Length is a minor cost compared to a bug that still exists.
Correct. Patching the symptom for one observed input leaves the cause in place, so the same defect reappears for every other input that reaches it.
Incorrect. 4 is the number of iterations, not the accumulated total.
Incorrect. 6 is the value after three passes, one short.
Correct. Four passes each add 2 to a variable starting at 0, giving 8.
Incorrect. 2 is the value after one pass. The loop runs four times.
A program works on the developer's test data and fails for a classmate.
Which is the most productive first step?
Incorrect. Rewriting discards working code before anyone knows what is wrong.
Correct. A bug that appears for one person and not another is a difference in input or environment, so reproducing it on the failing input is the step that turns a report into something debuggable.
Incorrect. Comments describe intent and do not locate the defect.
Incorrect. Working on one set of inputs is exactly the situation in which a real bug hides.

ap-csp-course-bi2-binary-numbers-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 2.1 Exercise 2: Binary Numbers Applied Challenge","<style>
Six questions that make you convert, count, and reason about what a fixed number of bits can and cannot hold.
Back to the Topic 2.1 lessonAll Big Idea 2 topics
The quiz checks that you can convert. These check that you know what happens at the edges: overflow, rounding, and how many values a bit width buys you.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A system stores a value in 6 bits, unsigned. How many distinct values can it represent, and what is the largest?
Correct. n bits give 2 to the n values. 2 to the sixth is 64 values, running from 0 to 63.
Incorrect. The count is 64, but counting from 0 means the largest is 63, not 64.
Incorrect. The number of bits is not the number of values. Each bit doubles the count.
Incorrect. 32 is 2 to the fifth, which is 5 bits. Six bits is double that.
What is the decimal value of the binary number 10110?
Incorrect. 26 would be 11010, which reverses two of the middle digits.
Incorrect. 44 is 10110 shifted one place left, which is double the correct value.
Incorrect. 16 accounts only for the leading 1 and ignores the rest.
Correct. The place values are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The set bits are 16, 4, and 2, giving 22.
A counter stored in 4 unsigned bits currently holds 15. The program adds 1.
Which outcome and error type is correct?
Incorrect. Syntax errors are detected before running and are unrelated to values.
Incorrect. 4 bits hold 0 through 15. 16 is one past the maximum.
Correct. Overflow is exactly this: a computation whose result needs more bits than the representation provides.
Incorrect. Round-off applies to values with fractional parts that cannot be represented exactly. This is an integer past its maximum.
A student says any decimal number can be stored exactly if you use enough bits.
Incorrect. Adding bits improves precision but never reaches exactness for a value with no finite representation.
Correct. Any fixed size representation stores a finite set of values, so values outside that set are approximated. That approximation is round-off error.
Incorrect. Being less than 1 makes no difference. One third is a problem at any scale.
Incorrect. Binary represents fractions routinely. Exactness for every fraction is the part that fails.
An image is stored with 8 bits per color channel and three channels per pixel.
How many distinct colors can one pixel take?
Correct. Each channel independently takes 256 values, so 256 cubed is 16,777,216 combinations.
Incorrect. 24 is the total bit count, not the number of colors those bits encode.
Incorrect. 256 is the range of one channel. Three channels combine rather than replace one another.
Incorrect. Adding the channel ranges undercounts. Independent channels multiply.
A sensor reports a reading every second and each reading is stored in 2 bytes. About how much storage does one hour of readings need?
Incorrect. 3,600 bytes assumes one byte per reading, which is half the stated size.
Incorrect. 120 counts minutes rather than seconds.
Incorrect. This counts one bit per reading rather than two bytes.
Correct. One hour is 3,600 seconds, so 3,600 readings at 2 bytes each is 7,200 bytes.

ap-csp-course-bi2-data-compression-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 2.2 Exercise 2: Data Compression Applied Challenge","<style>
Six scenarios where you must choose lossy or lossless, and defend the choice against the actual use.
Back to the Topic 2.2 lessonAll Big Idea 2 topics
The exam rarely asks what lossless means. It asks which one you would use here, and why the other one would be wrong.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A hospital archives patient scan images for later diagnosis.
Which compression choice is correct, and why?
Correct. Lossless compression reconstructs the original exactly. When any discarded detail could matter, that guarantee is the requirement.
Incorrect. The display is not the only consumer. The image may be enlarged, reprocessed, or re-examined later.
Incorrect. Medical data compresses like any other data. The question is only which kind.
Incorrect. Storage savings do not justify discarding information that cannot be recovered when the stakes are a diagnosis.
A student compresses a text file with a lossless method, then compresses the result again with the same method.
What is the most likely outcome of the second pass?
Incorrect. Lossless compression is reversible by definition, and applying it twice does not destroy the data.
Incorrect. The method does not change character based on how many times it is applied.
Incorrect. Compression is not a repeatable halving. The first pass consumed the pattern the method depends on.
Correct. Lossless methods shrink data by encoding redundancy compactly. Once removed, there is little left for a second pass to find.
A song is compressed from 40 MB to 4 MB and listeners cannot hear a difference.
Incorrect. Playback does not degrade a file. Repeated re-compression would.
Incorrect. Lossless is about whether the original can be reconstructed, not about whether a person notices.
Correct. A tenfold reduction on audio comes from discarding data. Imperceptible loss is still loss, and it is permanent.
Incorrect. Exact reconstruction is precisely what lossy compression gives up.
A program's source code is emailed as a compressed archive.
Why must this compression be lossless?
Incorrect. File size does not determine which compression is safe.
Correct. Code has no tolerance for approximation. One changed character is a different program, so the reconstruction must be exact.
Incorrect. Lossy methods can be applied to text. The result is simply useless, which is the point.
Incorrect. Email carries whatever bytes it is given. There is no such protocol rule.
A 12 MB file is compressed to 3 MB. What fraction of the original size remains, and what is the reduction?
Correct. 3 of 12 is one quarter remaining, so 9 of the 12 MB were removed, which is a 75 percent reduction.
Incorrect. One third of 12 is 4, not 3.
Incorrect. This reverses what remains and what was removed.
Incorrect. The remaining fraction is right but the reduction is its complement, not the same number.
A team must send video over a slow connection during a live stream.
Which reasoning best supports lossy compression here?
Incorrect. Lossless video compression exists. It simply does not shrink the data enough for this constraint.
Incorrect. Compression reduces the bandwidth needed. It does not eliminate the need for bandwidth.
Incorrect. Computation speed varies by method and is not the deciding argument here.
Correct. The tradeoff is fidelity against size, and in a live stream timely delivery is the requirement that fidelity is traded for.

ap-csp-course-bi2-extracting-information-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 2.3 Exercise 2: Extracting Information from Data Applied Challenge","<style>
Six scenarios about what a dataset can honestly support, and where a conclusion outruns the evidence.
Back to the Topic 2.3 lessonAll Big Idea 2 topics
Every question here has a tempting answer that the data almost supports. Finding the gap between correlation, sample, and claim is the skill.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A dataset shows that months with higher ice cream sales also have more swimming pool injuries.
Incorrect. This is the same causal overreach in the other direction.
Incorrect. Unrelated variables moving together is common and expected, not evidence of a data error.
Incorrect. A correlation alone never establishes which variable causes which, or that either does.
Correct. Correlation is a real pattern in the data. Attributing it to a shared cause is the standard and correct reading here.
A school surveys students about lunch preferences using a form linked from the yearbook club page.
Which limitation most affects conclusions drawn from the results?
Incorrect. Surveys produce numeric data routinely.
Incorrect. The correlation and causation distinction is real but is not what the sampling flaw affects here.
Correct. Who could reach the survey determines who answered, and a conclusion about all students needs a sample that reflects all students.
Incorrect. Volume is a processing concern, not a validity concern, and nothing suggests the volume is a problem.
A photo file carries the date, camera model, and location where it was taken.
What is this information called, and why does it matter for analysis?
Incorrect. The payload is the image itself. This is data describing that image.
Correct. Metadata is data about data, and it is what makes a large collection searchable and groupable at scale.
Incorrect. Compression details are separate and are not what date and location are.
Incorrect. A checksum verifies integrity and carries no descriptive meaning.
A student filters a sales dataset to rows where the region is North, then reports the average sale.
Correct. A statistic computed after filtering describes only the filtered subset. Extending it to the whole dataset is the common error.
Incorrect. The most common value is the mode, which is a different statistic from the average.
Incorrect. A total and an average are different summaries of the same rows.
Incorrect. Filtering removed every other region from the calculation.
A dataset of 500 rows has a blank value in the age column for 60 rows.
Which approach is most defensible when computing an average age?
Incorrect. Discarding 440 usable rows over 60 incomplete ones destroys far more information than it protects.
Incorrect. Inventing values, especially extreme ones, biases the result in a way no reader can detect.
Incorrect. Zero is a real age value, so treating missing data as zero drags the average down and misrepresents the data.
Correct. Excluding incomplete rows and stating that you did so keeps the statistic honest and lets a reader judge it.
A city wants to know which streets need repaving and uses reports submitted through a smartphone app.
Which bias is most likely in the resulting data?
Incorrect. Compression is unrelated to how the reports were gathered.
Incorrect. Duplicates are possible but are a cleaning problem, not the structural bias here.
Correct. Data collected through a device reflects who owns and uses that device, so need and reporting come apart in exactly the places least able to report.
Incorrect. Nothing about app-based reporting invents streets.

ap-csp-course-bi2-using-programs-with-data-exercise-2,"MERGE","AP CSP 2.4 Exercise 2: Using Programs with Data Applied Challenge","<style>
Six scenarios about cleaning, transforming, and scaling data processing beyond what a person could do by hand.
Back to the Topic 2.4 lessonAll Big Idea 2 topics
This topic is about the moment a dataset gets too big for a human. These questions ask what the program must do that the person no longer can.

column3: every answer is recorded for your teacher

column1: A dataset lists states as NY, N.Y., and New York across different rows.
What must happen before the rows can be grouped by state, and what is that step called?
Incorrect. Compression changes the size of the data, not the consistency of its values.
Correct. Cleaning resolves inconsistent representations of the same value so a grouping operation can see them as one thing.
Incorrect. Sorting arranges rows and does not merge different spellings, and it is not what filtering means.
Incorrect. Deleting the column removes the ability to group by state entirely.
A student processes 3 million rows by hand in a spreadsheet and gives up after a week.
Which statement best captures why a program is the right tool?
Correct. The argument for programs on large datasets is that they make an otherwise impossible amount of repeated work feasible.
Incorrect. Programs execute the analysis a person specifies. They do not supply the questions.
Incorrect. Cleaning is work a program does, not work a program removes.
Incorrect. On one row a careful person is just as accurate. Scale is the difference, not per row accuracy.
Temperatures are stored in Celsius and a report needs Fahrenheit.
What kind of operation is applied to the column, and what happens to the row count?
Incorrect. Compression is about storage size, not unit conversion.
Incorrect. Sorting reorders rows without changing any value.
Incorrect. A filter selects rows. Converting units selects nothing.
Correct. Transforming a column computes a new value for each row, so every row survives with a changed value.
A program filters a 100,000 row dataset to the 2,000 rows from last month, then computes a total.
Incorrect. Filtering keeps matching rows rather than removing them.
Incorrect. Filtering determines what the computation sees, so hidden rows are excluded from the total.
Correct. A computation after a filter describes exactly the filtered subset, which here is last month.
Incorrect. Filtering produces a subset for analysis and does not destroy the source data.
A program must find every row where the score is above 90 AND the region is West. Which describes what it does per row?
Incorrect. That describes OR, which would keep far more rows than intended.
Correct. A filter combining conditions with AND keeps a row only when every condition holds for it.
Incorrect. Ignoring the second condition would return West and non West rows alike.
Incorrect. Marking is not filtering. A filter narrows the set the later computation sees.
A visualization shows sales rising steeply, but the vertical axis starts at 90 rather than 0.
What is the most accurate criticism?
Correct. Starting an axis above zero stretches small differences across the full height of the chart, which misleads without any number being wrong.
